newsitem.title: JORDAN: King Hussein fears for future of Middle East peace.
newsitem.headline: King Hussein fears for future of Middle East peace.

text.p: Jordan's King Hussein on Wednesday voiced deep concern about the fate of the Middle East peace process after bomb attacks in a west Jerusalem street market killed at least 14 people.

"This incident which took place in Jerusalem which caused many victims to fall ... this latest incident, I do not know what its results will be," King Hussein said in a speech to graduates of Jordan's military academy broadcast by state television.

While a majority of Arabs and Israelis stood against violence and for peace, the monarch said the actions of "enemies of peace" on both sides of the divide who were bent on wrecking co-existence had a profound impact on course of developments.
"These are all crimes committed by a small group here and there but their impact is always great because it's an attempt to try to impose their agenda on the majority," he added.

The monarch said frustration brought about by the lack of progress in the Middle East peace process could have precipitated the bombing attack, in which 14 people were killed, including the two suicide bombers, and over 150 injured.

"Its causes could be a slowdown in what had been agreed to be implemented on the Palestinian-Israeli front and slowness in moving forward which some may have interpreted as an attempt to put an end to the move towards peace," the monarch said.
Jordan supports the Palestinian stance that Israel has been footdragging on implementing a 1993 interim self-rule peace accord.

Officials privately say the Israeli government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is not serious about advancing the peace process and is destroying what remaining hope there is by its accelerated Jewish settlement drive in the West Bank. said.
Jordan is increasingly worried about the repercussions of escalating violence in Palestinian territories on its own stability.

The kingdom's 4.2 million population have close ethnic ties with their Palestinian compatriots in the West Bank and Gaza. Earlier a government spokesman was quoted by the state news agency Petra as blaming the the attack on extremists who seek to wreck efforts to push the Middle East peace process forward.

Jordan, which signed its own peace treaty with Israel in 1994, expressed optimism on Tuesday about prospects of relaunching Israeli-Palestinian peace talks after Israel halted plans for a new Jewish settler enclave in Jerusalem.
But Jordan urged Israel not to give extremists what they wanted by being pushed by the attack to halt the peace process with the Palestinians, the spokesman said.
"Such terrorist attacks should only be a motive to resume negotiations and revitalise the stalled peace talks, not obstruct it," the official spokesman said.
"This is important to prevent the enemies of peace from attaining their aim," he added.
